Does not understand English, but bases his judgment on the intonation.

“Alberto Montani, confectioner, states that he was among the first people to climb the stairs. Heard the voices described. The deep, rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. Recognized several words. The speaker seemed to be protesting. Could not distinguish any words spoken by the shrill voice, which was rapid and uneven. Believes it was a Russian voice. Confirms the general testimony. Is Italian. Has never spoken with a native Russian.

“Several witnesses, called back for further questioning, testified here that the chimneys in every fourth-floor room were too narrow for a human being to pass through. By ‘sweeps’ they meant the cylindrical brushes used by chimney cleaners. These brushes were pushed up and down every flue in the house. There is no rear passage by which anyone could have come downstairs while the group was going up. Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was wedged so tightly in the chimney that four or five people had to combine their strength to pull it down.

“Paul Dumas, physician, states that he was summoned to examine the bodies at about dawn. Both were then lying on the bedstead’s canvas support in the room where Mademoiselle L. had been discovered. The young woman’s body was extensively bruised and scraped. Being forced up the chimney would adequately explain these marks. Her throat was badly grazed. Several deep scratches appeared just below her chin, along with a row of dark bruises that were clearly finger marks. Her face was horribly discolored, and her eyeballs bulged. Her tongue had been partly bitten through. A large bruise at the pit of her stomach appeared to have been caused by pressure from a knee. In M. Dumas’s opinion, Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been strangled by an unknown person or persons. Her mother’s body was terribly mutilated. Every bone in her right arm and leg was shattered to some degree. The left shinbone was badly splintered, as were all the ribs on her left side. The entire body was severely bruised and discolored. It was impossible to determine exactly how these injuries had been inflicted. A heavy wooden club, a broad iron bar, a chair—any large, heavy, blunt weapon could have caused them if wielded by a very powerful man. No woman could have delivered such blows with any weapon. When the witness saw the deceased, her head had been completely separated from her body and was itself badly shattered. Her throat had plainly been cut with a very sharp instrument, probably a razor.

Colonel Grangerford was a gentleman, you see. He was a gentleman in every way, and his whole family was the same. He came from a good family, as people say, and that matters as much in a man as in a horse, according to the Widow Douglas. Nobody ever questioned that she was among the finest people in our town. Pap always said it too, though he himself had no more class than a mudcat. Colonel Grangerford was very tall and thin, with skin that was somehow both dark and pale, without a touch of red anywhere. His narrow face was shaved clean every morning. He had extremely thin lips and narrow nostrils, a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and the blackest eyes you could imagine. They were set so deep that they seemed to stare at you from inside caves. He had a high forehead, and his straight black hair hung to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin. Every single day he wore a clean shirt and a full linen suit so white it hurt your eyes to look at it. On Sundays he wore a blue coat with tails and brass buttons. His cane was mahogany with a silver top. There was nothing silly about him, nothing at all, and he never raised his voice. He was wonderfully kind; you could feel that, and it made you trust him. Sometimes he smiled, and that was a lovely sight. But when he stood straight as a flagpole and his eyes flashed beneath those eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and ask what was wrong afterward. He never needed to remind anyone of their manners. Everybody behaved politely around him. People loved having him nearby, too. He was usually like sunshine—I mean, he made you feel the weather was good. When he turned into a storm cloud, things got terribly dark for half a minute. That was enough; nothing would go wrong again for a week.

When he and his wife came downstairs in the morning, everyone in the family stood up and greeted them. Nobody sat down until the two of them had taken their seats. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the liquor bottle stood, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held his drink while they mixed their own. Then they bowed and said, “Our respects to you, sir and madam.” The older couple bowed very slightly and thanked them, and all three men drank. Bob and Tom added a spoonful of water to the sugar and the little bit of whisky or apple brandy left in their glasses and gave them to Buck and me, so we toasted the older people too.

Mr. Bennet hardly spoke during dinner. Once the servants had left, though, he decided it was time to talk to his guest. He chose a subject on which he expected him to do well, remarking how lucky he seemed in the wealthy lady who supported him. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort seemed quite remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen a better topic. Mr. Collins praised her at length. It made his manner even more solemn than usual, and with an air of great importance he declared that he had never seen anyone of high rank behave with such friendliness and willingness to notice a person below her. Lady Catherine had kindly approved both sermons he had so far had the honor of preaching before her. She had invited him to dinner at Rosings twice and had sent for him only the previous Saturday to complete her evening card game of quadrille. He knew many people thought Lady Catherine proud, but he had found her nothing but friendly. She always addressed him as she would any gentleman. She raised no objection to his socializing in the neighborhood, or occasionally leaving his parish for a week or two to visit relatives. She had even kindly advised him to marry as soon as possible, as long as he chose carefully. Once she had visited his modest parsonage, fully approved the changes he was making, and even suggested some herself: shelves in the upstairs cupboards.

“That all sounds very proper and polite,” Mrs. Bennet said, “and I’m sure she is a very pleasant woman. It’s a pity more great ladies aren’t like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“Only a lane separates the garden around my humble home from Rosings Park, her ladyship’s residence.”

“I believe you said she was a widow, sir. Does she have any children?”

“She has just one daughter, who will inherit Rosings and a very large amount of property.”

“Ah,” Mrs. Bennet cried, shaking her head, “then she is better provided for than many girls. And what is she like? Is she pretty?”

“She is a most charming young lady. Lady Catherine herself says that in true beauty Miss de Bourgh is far above even the most beautiful women, because her features possess something that clearly identifies a young woman of noble birth.
